prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B027 with Autor, Hanson and Katz, and the same citation. The exchange tested it and did not weaken it. Two things changed in my reading. First, the round-1 files show that Enflo and Krusell now name the same three-person set, so the live attribution question is a choice about the scope of the citation, not a split among members. Second, the chair's questions pushed me to state Katz's contribution concretely. From my own knowledge, and without independent verification, his distinct and citable contribution is the supply-and-demand account of the skill premium (Katz-Murphy lineage), the education-versus-technology framing of long-run wage-structure change, and the work on polarisation with Autor. That is evidence on why the wage structure moves. The China-shock papers are evidence on how and where adjustment happens and what it costs. The two together answer one question, who gains and who loses when technology and trade shift labour demand. The identification is design-based throughout, which I treat as the central test of whether a causal claim has been established. The core findings have been replicated and contested for a decade or more, and the contest has refined magnitudes and heterogeneity without overturning the qualitative result of slow, concentrated, costly adjustment. I wrote this citation around labour demand, wages and local labour markets, not around the task model as theory. That wording makes no claim of theoretical priority over Acemoglu, Levy or Murnane. It also keeps the claim on empirical demonstration, which is where the credited names are strongest. My ranking rests on the standard I would apply to any candidate: a credible answer to an important causal question, a framework that organises the evidence, and durability under reanalysis.
statement.case_against: Attribution under the three-name cap is still the weakest point. Dorn is a central co-author of the trade-shock papers and is excluded. If the committee reads the achievement as the import-competition work only, Autor, Dorn and Hanson is the better set and my Katz version would credit a strand the citation does not name. The citation also joins two literatures with different identification strategies and partly different authors, and a committee could reasonably call that two prizes joined by Autor. On marginal novelty, the education-versus-technology framing is associated with Goldin and Katz, and Goldin was recognised in 2023, so the committee would have to say what is separately new. The 2021 prize I presented concerned causal-inference methods and applied work on minimum wages, immigration and education, and the 2024 prize touched technology and institutions. These are adjacent, not identical, but the overlap argument is real. The magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects, and their external validity beyond the US episode, remain debated. The designs also identify local effects. Aggregate welfare statements need more structure than the evidence alone supplies.

responses.point: Krusell's round-1 file moves from B012 to B027 and names Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues that the Katz strand is needed so the citation covers both technology and trade, and that the China-shock critiques refine the finding rather than overturn it. He also notes that B012 has crowded credit (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum) and sits next to the 2008 prize.
responses.response: I misread your position in round 1. I treated you as proposing Autor and Hanson alone, and the file says otherwise. I welcome the move, and I agree with your reasoning on Katz and on how to read the critiques. I also agree that B012's precursor credit is a real obstacle, which is why I keep it only as a second alternative. I withdraw the earlier suggestion that a two-person award is your preferred route. I still regard Autor and Hanson as a defensible fallback if the committee finds three-way credit too diffuse. I would rather the committee choose that fallback explicitly, after testing the three-name citation, than drift into it.

responses.point: Enflo's round-1 file moves from Autor, Dorn and Hanson to Autor, Hanson and Katz, because a citation covering technology and trade needs the skills-and-technology anchor. She also proposes wording the citation around labour demand and adjustment, and not around the task model, to avoid claiming theoretical priority.
responses.response: My round-1 reply addressed your opening trio, which your file no longer proposes. We now agree on the set and on the wording. Your point that the citation should say 'adjustment' and not a particular effect size is the right protection against the China-shock magnitude critiques, and I adopt it in my reading of the citation. I would add one condition. The wording works only if the committee accepts that the technology and trade strands are one question about labour demand. If it does not, your original trio is the right fallback. I would support that trio over a muddled joint citation.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He argues that the mechanism is foundational, the attribution is clean, and the 2022 prize covered banks and runs, not asset-price-driven collateral amplification. As chair he also asks whether B006's thinner identification is disqualifying or only a reason to rank it lower.
responses.response: It is a reason to rank it lower, not a disqualifier. I accept that the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is dynamic and works through asset prices, and that it differs from the 2022 work on runs and intermediation. Stromberg makes this point too. The part of the 2022 overlap that still concerns me is the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator lineage, because a citation would have to say plainly what is new. That is why I keep B006 as my first alternative. If attribution proves fatal for B027, I would vote for B006 with Kiyotaki and Moore as a defensible result. On the evidence in front of us, the empirical confirmation behind B027 is broader and more directly tested. I do not read your first-place ranking as a field bias. It reflects the weight you put on a clean originator pair, which is a legitimate criterion.

responses.point: Teorell prefers Katz over Dorn because he wants the citation to cover technology and skills as well as trade. He concedes that if the committee narrows the citation to trade exposure, he would support Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He also says the discovery is the easiest on the shortlist to state in one citation.
responses.response: I agree with both the preference and the concession, and my own position has the same structure. The choice between Katz and Dorn follows from what the citation says, not from a view about whose work is better. Where I would press you is the 'easiest to state' claim. It holds only if the committee accepts that the two strands are one achievement, so it is a conclusion of the argument and not a premise. I have tried to support that conclusion by pointing to the common question and the common object of measurement, namely wage and employment responses of skill groups and places. I would want the committee to vote on that scope question explicitly, since it decides between our two trios.

responses.point: Friberg's round-1 file also names Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues that a trade-shock-only trio would credit one half of the achievement. He says he would word the citation around findings on labour demand, wages and local labour markets, and he accepts that Dorn's exclusion is a real cost.
responses.response: We now hold the same configuration, and I agree with the wording principle. Your point about the match between the credited work and the citation is the cleanest way to put the test. I would add something to your treatment of overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes. Since I presented the 2021 prize, I am conscious that the committee should not assume the overlap away. The distinction I rely on is that the 2021 prize rewarded identification methods and applied work on other questions, while B027 concerns the demand side of the wage structure and the cost of adjustment. If colleagues think that boundary is thinner than I do, the Goldin-Katz link is the point to examine.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the technology and trade strands as one achievement or two. This decides between Autor-Hanson-Katz and Autor-Dorn-Hanson, and I would back the second if the citation is narrowed to import competition.

How much of the education-versus-technology framing is separately new relative to Goldin's 2023 recognition, and how much of the task framework belongs to contributors outside the credited names, including Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane.
How robust the persistence, magnitude and external validity of the China-shock effects are, and how the committee should weigh new evidence on automation and AI.
Whether the committee would fall back to Autor and Hanson if three-way credit is judged too diffuse, or move to B006 or B012 instead.
My assessments rely on my own knowledge of the literature and the supplied files. I have not independently verified any claim, and I treat support counts as no evidence of merit.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from my profile, nor to the credited names of B006 or B012. My listed co-authors (Oosterbeek, van Ours, Holmlund, Edin, Åslund, Öckert, Johansson, Nybom) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. B027 and B028 are close to my own field of empirical labour economics, and my research follows the design-based tradition the 2021 Scientific Background describes. I disclose this as adjacency and as a possible lean toward design-based evidence, not as a connection. I gave the 2021 presentation speech as chair, which may make me more alert to overlap between B027 and that prize. Conflicts are disclosed, not adjudicated.
